summary: The second letter to TIP users from BBN, following RFC 365. BBN planned a series of such letters to document TIP system changes before the TIP User's Guide could be revised. It explains some changes, including ones suggested by users, such as the protocol to login command.

plainLanguage.summary: BBN's second letter to TIP users explains upcoming command changes and problems that could interrupt connections. It also describes login stages and ways users could recover from a login that seemed stuck.

subtitle: Updates and troubleshooting advice for TIP users

tldr.problem: TIP users needed current information about command changes and connection problems before the printed guide could be revised.
tldr.mechanism: BBN uses this letter to announce command changes, explain network failures and describe how the TIP login process works.
tldr.outcome: The letter gives users current instructions and reports known problems that BBN was investigating.

today: RFC 386 is a TIP user letter describing planned command changes and known operating problems. It gives the guidance available to users while BBN investigated those issues.

sections.title: TIP Commands and Messages
sections.content:
The letter says that the older @PROTOCOL TO LOGIN and @PROTOCOL TO CLOSE BOTH commands would be removed in favor of @LOGIN and @CLOSE. It describes planned changes to @LOGIN, @HOST and @TRANSMIT, including sending a message when the buffer was almost full.

BBN also planned a TIP GOING DOWN message before maintenance or software releases. The letter recommends keeping these updates with the TIP User's Guide until printed revisions were available.
sections.plainLanguage: Several TIP commands were changing, and a new message would warn users before planned shutdowns. BBN sent these letters so users could learn changes before a new guide was printed.

sections.title: Connections Interrupted by Network Problems
sections.content:
The letter explains that a brief network partition could make a TIP close a connection even while the host still believed it was open. A later login could then be refused because the host retained the earlier connection. Another failure could occur when an IMP crashed and a message was lost, leaving TIP and host allocation counters out of sync.

BBN describes possible recovery actions, including resetting connections through a Host/Host command or asking the host to log out a stuck job.
sections.plainLanguage: A temporary network failure could leave the TIP and host with different views of a connection. The letter describes ways to clear a stuck session, while noting that the available reset was broad.

sections.title: How the Login Queue Works
sections.content:
The letter divides opening a connection into three phases: waiting for the TIP logger, performing the login sequence, and waiting for the host to open data connections. Only one user could be in the login sequence at a time, and that phase could time out after about one minute. Waiting in the queue or waiting for the host could add further delay.

The behavior of Abort Login depends on which phase the user is in. The letter gives steps for interpreting the TIP's responses before trying again.
sections.plainLanguage: Logging in involves a queue, the login exchange and a wait for the host. The abort command behaves differently in each stage, so users were given instructions for checking what happened.

sections.title: Other User Guidance
sections.content:
BBN says the NEWS herald would be removed from the TIP's HELLO message because it could not tell when every user had read the news. The letter also warns hosts that send commands to TIPs that the TIP command language was changing and should be easy to update.

The DEVICE CODE EXECUPORT command would be renamed DEVICE CODE EXTRA-PADDING, a name intended to cover other terminals that needed the feature.
sections.plainLanguage: Users were told to check NEWS themselves, and host programs that send TIP commands should be easy to change. One device command was renamed to describe its broader use.
